pharm: Selectively blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors peripherally on vagal nerve terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, preventing chemotherapy- and radiation-induced emesis.
quick: 2 mg once daily or 1 mg twice daily on chemo/radiation days
May take with or without food
Animal data reassuring; use only if clearly needed
Excretion in milk unknown; use with caution
summary: Granisetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist used to prevent nausea and vomiting from emetogenic chemotherapy (including high-dose cisplatin) and radiation. It is generally well tolerated, requires no dose adjustment for renal or hepatic impairment, and carries risks of QT prolongation and serotonin syndrome, particularly with concomitant serotonergic drugs.
indications: Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with initial and repeat courses of emetogenic cancer chemotherapy, including high-dose cisplatin
Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with radiation, including total body irradiation and fractionated abdominal radiation

dosage.n: Given only on day(s) chemotherapy is administered

dosage.d: 1 mg orally, then 1 mg 12 hours later
dosage.t: First dose up to 1 hour before chemotherapy
dosage.n: Continued treatment between chemo cycles is not useful
Wide pharmacokinetic variability noted in hepatic impairment

admin: Administer up to 1 hour before chemotherapy (within 1 hour of radiation)
May be given with or without food
Oral solution: a 2 mg dose (10 mL) is bioequivalent to two 1 mg tablets and may be used interchangeably
Give only on day(s) of emetogenic therapy; do not continue between cycles
Assess QT risk factors before use, especially with cardiac disease or QT-prolonging drugs
moa: Granisetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist with little or no affinity for other serotonin, adrenergic, dopaminergic, histaminergic, benzodiazepine, or opioid receptors. Emetogenic chemotherapy and radiation cause release of serotonin from enterochromaffin cells of the small intestine; serotonin stimulates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the area postrema, evoking the vomiting reflex. Granisetron blocks this serotonin stimulation to prevent emesis.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to granisetron or any of its components
relative: Pre-existing arrhythmias or cardiac conduction disorders
Congenital long QT syndrome or electrolyte abnormalities
monitor: ECG in patients with QT risk factors
Signs of masked progressive ileus or gastric distention after abdominal surgery

preg: Pregnancy Category B (older labeling). Animal reproduction studies in rats and rabbits at doses far exceeding the human dose revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or fetal harm. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: It is not known whether granisetron is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk, exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: Total clearance of granisetron was not affected in patients with severe renal failure. No dosage adjustment is recommended.
hepatic: In patients with hepatic impairment due to neoplastic liver involvement, total clearance was approximately halved; however, given the wide pharmacokinetic variability, no dosage adjustment is necessary.

major: Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, mirtazapine, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, IV methylene blue) - serotonin syndrome, sometimes fatal
QT-prolonging / arrhythmogenic drugs - additive risk of clinically significant QT prolongation
moderate: Strong hepatic CYP enzyme inducers (e.g., phenobarbital) may increase clearance (~25% increase observed)
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) may inhibit metabolism (clinical significance unknown)
minor: No significant interaction with benzodiazepines, neuroleptics, or anti-ulcer agents
Does not appear to interact with emetogenic cancer chemotherapies
interactions.food: Food slightly decreases AUC (~5%) and increases Cmax (~30%); may be taken with or without food.

emergency: Serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability)

monitoring: ECG in patients with pre-existing arrhythmias, cardiac disease, electrolyte abnormalities, or on QT-prolonging/cardiotoxic drugs
Signs of serotonin syndrome, especially with concomitant serotonergic drugs
counsel: Report fast or irregular heartbeat, fainting, or dizziness
Report agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, or fever (possible serotonin syndrome)
Headache and constipation are the most common side effects
Take only on the days of chemotherapy or radiation as directed
Inform clinician of all medications, especially antidepressants and heart drugs
pk: Cmax ~3.6 ng/mL after a single 1 mg oral dose
~6.2 hours (volunteers); longer in elderly; ~9 h after IV
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep tightly closed, upright; protect from light
pearls: Once-daily 2 mg and twice-daily 1 mg regimens are comparably effective
No dose adjustment needed for renal failure, hepatic impairment, or age
Give only on treatment days; continued dosing between cycles is not useful
QT prolongation reported; use caution with cardiac disease or QT-prolonging drugs
Serotonin syndrome can occur, especially with other serotonergic agents
missed: Used as scheduled prophylaxis on treatment days only. If a dose is missed, take when remembered unless near the next planned dose; do not double up. Confirm timing with the oncology team.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Overdoses up to 38.5 mg of granisetron hydrochloride (injection) have been reported with no symptoms or only a slight headache. Manage symptomatically with supportive care.
